messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual/Bodily Cues: Blood, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rana is a 21-year-old forester who came to treatment months after witnessing a fatal road accident on a narrow service road at the edge of state woodland where she works. She had been driving between survey points when she came upon two cars that had collided head-on. One driver was slumped over the wheel, bleeding heavily; in the other car a young passenger was crying and trying to get out. Rana remembers the red on the dashboard and on her hands after she tried to help, the sharp smell of gasoline and hot metal in the summer air, and people shouting for someone to call 911. What has stayed with her most is the conviction that she did not do enough. She had come to believe she should have protected the people there and failed, and that in those confused minutes she acted against the kind of person she thought she was.

In the weeks afterward, ordinary parts of work and daily life began to pull her back toward the scene. Seeing blood, even from a minor cut in the field, made her stomach drop. Passing wrecked cars on the highway or even seeing images of cars hit in accidents could stop her cold. If coworkers started talking about crashes, she would feel herself tense before she could think. In those moments the memory did not arrive as a clear story. Instead it came in fragments, along with the smell from the accident, so vivid that for a second she felt she was breathing it again. At the same time, the memory felt strangely unreal, as if it belonged to someone else rather than to her, and she would push it away before it could come fully into focus. Those same triggers also brought back her harshest conclusions about herself: that she had failed to protect others, that something in her had been exposed as inadequate, and that the happy version of herself was gone.

Rana began arranging her life around not being caught off guard. At work, where she spends long stretches driving logging roads and walking isolated tracts, she started scanning constantly for signs of danger—vehicles coming too fast around a bend, sounds from the road, anything out of place in the trees. If colleagues began swapping stories about accidents during lunch, she would leave or shut the conversation down. At night she delayed sleep for hours, keeping videos on or scrolling on her phone until she was exhausted enough to drop off. Part of this was fear of what would come when things got quiet: whenever she let herself settle, the smell and scattered images pressed closer. Part of it was also punishment. She was certain she did not deserve rest when she had failed people who needed help.

These habits did not calm things for long. The more she pushed away reminders and cut off conversations, the less the event felt like something that had happened and ended, and the more it returned as disconnected flashes with that same intrusive smell. Staying up late left her worn down and more vulnerable to being jolted by images of damaged cars the next day. Constantly checking her surroundings kept her attention fixed on the possibility of another crash, so roadside details that others barely noticed stood out to her immediately and set off the same cascade. In this way, the very things she did to keep control seemed to make the memory more brittle and alien, and each new jolt was taken as further proof that she was no longer the happy, capable person she used to be.

Over time, the effects became visible in her work. Forestry had once felt grounding to Rana; now even routine field days could feel like exposure to danger. She took longer routes to avoid certain roads and was distracted during site checks because she was watching for threats rather than focusing on the land. She kept more to herself with coworkers, partly to avoid any mention of accidents, partly because she felt ashamed of how much she had changed. When blood was mentioned or a vehicle with front-end damage appeared at a gas station, she could feel the smell come back before the rest of the scene, and with it the sense that she had failed at a basic human duty.

By the time she sought help, Rana was exhausted from sleeping only in the early morning hours and from living in a state of alertness that never fully switched off. She did not come in saying she wanted to “process trauma.” She said she was scared that if she let the memory come all the way through, it would confirm what she already believed—that she had failed people and become someone she could not respect. At the same time, a small part of her was hoping to feel like herself again, or at least to learn how to be in the woods, on the road, and in her own mind without bracing for the accident to happen all over again.
